title: III. The Schoolboy
paragraphs: But Kolya didn't hear her. At last he could leave. As he stepped through the gate he looked around, shrugged his shoulders, muttered “It's freezing,” and walked straight down the street, turning right toward the marketplace. At the last house before the market he stopped at the gate, pulled a whistle from his pocket, and blew on it with all his strength as though sending a signal. He didn't have to wait more than a minute before a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven, in a warm, neat, even stylish coat, came darting out to meet him. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin), the son of a well-to-do official. Apparently his parents had forbidden him to keep company with Krassotkin, who was known around town as a desperately naughty boy, so Smurov was clearly sneaking out. He was — in case the reader has forgotten — one of the group of boys who two months earlier had thrown stones at Ilusha. He was also the one who had told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
“I've been waiting for you for the last hour, Krassotkin,” Smurov said stolidly, and the two boys set off toward the marketplace.
“I'm late,” Krassotkin answered. “I was held up by circumstances. You won't get thrashed for coming with me, will you?”
“Come on, I never get thrashed! And you've brought Perezvon?”
“Yes.”
“You're bringing him too?”
“Yes.”
“Ah, if only it were Zhutchka!”
“Impossible. Zhutchka doesn't exist. Zhutchka is lost in the mists of oblivion.”
“Ah — couldn't we try this?” Smurov stopped suddenly. “Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog like Perezvon. Couldn't you tell him this is Zhutchka? Maybe he'd believe you.”
“My boy, steer clear of lying, that's one thing; and steer clear of it even for a good cause, that's another. Above all, I hope you haven't told them anything about my coming.”

“Heaven forbid! I know what I'm doing. But Perezvon won't comfort him,” Smurov said with a sigh. “You know his father, the captain — the one they call ‘the wisp of tow’ — told us today he's bringing Ilusha a real mastiff puppy, black-nosed, the works. He thinks it will comfort Ilusha, but I doubt it.”
“And how is Ilusha?”

“Bad, very bad. I think he has consumption. He's quite conscious, but his breathing — his breathing is all wrong. The other day he asked to have his boots put on so he could be led around the room. He tried to walk but couldn't stand up. ‘Ah, I told you before, father,’ he said, ‘that those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.’ He thought it was the boots making him stagger, but it was just weakness. He won't last another week. Herzenstube is looking after him. They've got money again now — heaps of it.”
“They're crooks.”
“Who are crooks?”

“Doctors, and the whole tribe of quacks — collectively, and individually, of course. I don't believe in medicine. It's a useless institution. I intend to look into all of that. But what's this sentimental business going on at your place? The whole class seems to be dropping by every day.”
“Not the whole class: only about ten of our fellows go to see him every day. That's nothing.”

“What I don't understand in all this is Alexey Karamazov's part in it. His brother is going to be tried tomorrow or the day after for such a crime, and he still has so much time to spend on sentimental visits with boys.”
“There's nothing sentimental about it. You're going yourself, right now, to patch things up with Ilusha.”
“Patch things up with him? What a ridiculous expression. But I don't let anyone analyze my actions.”
“And how thrilled Ilusha will be to see you! He has no idea you're coming. Why, why wouldn't you come all this time?” Smurov cried with sudden feeling.

“My dear boy, that's my business, not yours. I'm going on my own because I choose to, but the rest of you have been dragged there by Alexey Karamazov — there's a difference. And how do you know? Maybe I'm not going to patch anything up at all. It's a stupid expression.”

“It has nothing to do with Karamazov — it wasn't his doing. Our fellows started going on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. But there's been none of that kind of nonsense. One went, then another. His father was overjoyed to see us. You know he'll simply go out of his mind if Ilusha dies. He sees that Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we've made up with Ilusha. Ilusha asked after you, that was all. He just asks and says nothing more. His father will go out of his mind — or hang himself. He was behaving like a madman before. He's a decent man, really. We made a mistake then. It was all the fault of that murderer who beat him.”
“Karamazov is still a riddle to me. I could have made his acquaintance long ago, but I prefer to keep a certain pride in some cases. Besides, I have a theory about him I need to work out and verify.”

Kolya lapsed into dignified silence. Smurov kept quiet too. He worshipped Krassotkin and never dreamed of putting himself on the same footing. He was intensely curious now about Kolya's saying that he was going “on his own” to see Ilusha. He sensed some mystery in Kolya's sudden decision to come today. They crossed the marketplace, which at that hour was crowded with loaded wagons from the countryside and great numbers of live fowls. Market women sat in their booths selling rolls, cotton, thread, and the like. These Sunday markets were naively called “fairs” in town, and there were many such fairs in the course of the year.
Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing first one side, then the other. When he met other dogs they eagerly sniffed each other over according to the rules of canine etiquette.
“I like watching scenes like this, Smurov,” Kolya said suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”
“Yes, it's a funny habit.”

“No, it's not funny — you're wrong there. There's nothing funny in nature, however funny it may look to man with all his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they'd certainly find just as much — if not far more — to laugh at in the social relations between humans, their masters. Far more, in fact. I'll say it again, because I'm convinced there's far more foolishness among us. That's Rakitin's idea — a remarkable one. I'm a Socialist, Smurov.”
“And what's a Socialist?” Smurov asked.

“It's when everyone is equal and everyone shares property in common, there are no marriages, and everyone follows any religion and laws he likes, and so on. You're not old enough to understand all that yet. It's cold, though.”
“Yes — twelve degrees of frost. Father just checked the thermometer.”

“Have you noticed, Smurov, how in the middle of winter we don't feel the cold even at fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost as much as we do now, at the start of winter, when there's a sudden twelve-degree freeze — especially when there isn't much snow yet? It's because people aren't used to it. Everything is habit with human beings — even in their social and political relations. Habit is the great motive power. What a funny-looking peasant!”

Kolya pointed at a tall peasant with a good-natured face in a long sheepskin coat, standing beside his wagon, clapping his hands in shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was all white with frost.
“That peasant's beard is frozen,” Kolya shouted in a loud, provocative voice as he passed him.
“Lots of people's beards are frozen,” the peasant replied calmly and sententiously.
“Don't provoke him,” Smurov said.
“It's all right — he won't get angry. He's a decent fellow. Good-bye, Matvey.”
“Good-bye.”
“Is your name Matvey?”
“Yes. Didn't you know?”
“No, I didn't. It was a guess.”
“You don't say! You're a schoolboy, I take it?”
“Yes.”
“And you get whipped, I expect?”
“Nothing much — now and then.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Well, yes, it does.”
“Ech, what a life!” the peasant sighed from the bottom of his heart.
“Good-bye, Matvey.”
“Good-bye. You're a nice lad, that you are.”
The boys walked on.
“That was a nice peasant,” Kolya observed to Smurov. “I enjoy talking with peasants, and I'm always happy to give them their due.”
“Why did you lie and tell him we get thrashed?” Smurov asked.
“I had to say it to please him.”
“How do you mean?”

“Smurov, I don't like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on the first time. Some things can't be explained. In a peasant's mind, schoolboys are whipped — and ought to be. What sort of schoolboy would one be if he weren't whipped? And if I had told him we aren't, he'd have been disappointed. But you don't understand that. You have to know how to talk to peasants.”
“Just don't tease them, please, or you'll land in another scrape, like that business with the goose.”
“So you're scared?”
“Don't laugh, Kolya. Of course I'm scared. My father would be furious. I'm strictly forbidden to go out with you.”
“Don't worry — nothing will happen this time. Hey there, Natasha!” he shouted to a market woman in one of the booths.
“Calling me Natasha! Really! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged market woman shouted back at him.
“I'm glad it's Marya. Good-bye!”
“Ah, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on so!”
“I'm in a hurry. I can't stop. You can tell me next Sunday.” Kolya waved her off as though she had attacked him and not the other way around.
“I've nothing to tell you next Sunday. You jumped on me, you impudent little monkey. I said nothing,” Marya bellowed. “You need a whipping, that's what you need, you saucy jackanapes!”

There was a roar of laughter from the other market women around her. Suddenly a man in a fit of rage burst out from the arcade of shops nearby. He was a young man, not a native of the town, with dark, curly hair and a long, pale face pitted with smallpox scars. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap and looked like a merchant's clerk. He was in a state of stupid excitement and was brandishing his fist at Kolya.
“I know you!” he cried angrily. “I know you!”
Kolya stared at him. He couldn't recall ever having a row with this man. But he'd been in so many street rows he could hardly keep track of them all.
“Do you?” he asked sarcastically.
“I know you! I know you!” the man repeated idiotically.
“All the better for you. Well, it's time I was off. Good-bye!”
“At your saucy pranks again?” the man cried. “At your saucy pranks again? I know it, you're at it again!”
“It's not your business, brother, whether I'm at my saucy pranks or not,” Kolya said, standing his ground and sizing him up.
“Not my business?”
“No, not your business.”
“Whose then? Whose then? Whose then?”
“It's Trifon Nikititch's business, not yours.”
“What Trifon Nikititch?” the young man asked, staring at Kolya with loutish amazement, though still just as angry.
Kolya looked him over gravely.
“Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he asked suddenly, with stern emphasis.
“What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven't,” the young man said, thrown off a little.
“Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya went on, even more emphatically, even more severely.
“What Sabaneyev? No, I don't know him.”

“Then you can go to the devil,” Kolya said, cutting the exchange short; and turning sharply to the right he strode quickly on his way as though he disdained any further conversation with a dolt who didn't even know Sabaneyev.
“Stop — hey! What Sabaneyev?” the young man cried, jolted out of his stupor and as worked up as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women with a foolish stare.
The women laughed.
“There's no telling what he's up to,” said one.
“What Sabaneyev is it he's talking about?” the young man kept repeating, still furious and shaking his right arm.
“It must be a Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs — that must be who it is,” one of the women suggested.
The young man gave her a wild stare.
“For the Kuzmitchovs?” another woman repeated. “But his name wasn't Trifon. His name's Kuzma, not Trifon; and the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can't be the same man.”

“His name isn't Trifon, and it isn't Sabaneyev — it's Tchizhov,” a third woman put in suddenly. She had been silent until then, listening gravely. “Alexey Ivanitch is his first name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”
“Of course — it's Tchizhov,” a fourth woman confirmed emphatically.
The bewildered youth looked from one to another.
“But what did he want with me? What did he want with me, good people?” he cried almost in desperation. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ he says. And who the devil can know who Sabaneyev is?”
“You're a fool. I'm telling you it's not Sabaneyev, it's Tchizhov — Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that's who it is!” one of the women shouted at him impressively.
“What Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”
“That tall, sniveling fellow who used to sit in the market in the summer.”
“And what's your Tchizhov got to do with me, good people, eh?”

“How should I know what he's got to do with you?” another put in. “You ought to know for yourself what you want with him, if you're going to raise such a racket about him. He was talking to you, not to us, you fool. Don't you really know him?”
“Know whom?”
“Tchizhov.”
“To the devil with Tchizhov and you along with him. I'll give him a hiding, that I will. He was making fun of me!”
“Give Tchizhov a hiding? More likely he'll give you one. You're a fool, that's what you are!”
“Not Tchizhov — not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischievous woman. I'll give the boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

The woman guffawed. But Kolya was already far off by now, marching along with a triumphant air. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group behind them. He too was in high spirits, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya's company.
“What Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, guessing what the answer would be.

“How should I know? Now there'll be a commotion among them all day. I like stirring up fools in every class of society. There's another blockhead, that peasant over there. They say ‘there's no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,' but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just as much. Can't you see all over his face that peasant's a fool, eh?”
“Leave him alone, Kolya. Let's keep going.”
“Nothing can stop me now that I've got started. Hey, good morning, peasant!”
A sturdy peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard, walking past, raised his head and looked at the boy. He didn't seem quite sober.
“Good morning, if you aren't laughing at me,” he said deliberately in reply.
“And what if I am?” Kolya laughed.
“Well, a joke's a joke. Laugh away. I don't mind. There's no harm in a joke.”
“I beg your pardon, brother, it was a joke.”
“Well, God forgive you.”
“Do you forgive me too?”
“I forgive you entirely. Be on your way.”
“I say, you seem to be a clever peasant.”
“Cleverer than you,” the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
“I doubt it,” Kolya said, somewhat taken aback.
“It's true, all the same.”
“Perhaps it is.”
“It is, brother.”
“Good-bye, peasant!”
“Good-bye!”
“There are all sorts of peasants,” Kolya observed to Smurov after a short silence. “How was I to know I'd landed on a clever one? I'm always ready to recognize intelligence in the peasantry.”

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half past eleven. The boys hurried and walked the considerable distance to Captain Snegiryov's lodgings quickly and almost without speaking. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go on ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
“One needs to sniff around a little first,” he remarked to Smurov.
“Why ask him to come out?” Smurov protested. “Just go in — they'll be overjoyed to see you. What's the sense of making friends in the frost out here?”
“I know why I want to see him out here in the frost,” Kolya cut him short in the despotic tone he liked to adopt with “small boys,” and Smurov ran off to do his bidding.
